analysis.one_liner: Voids EPA air-toxics rules for cement plants and delays compliance at least five years.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 262-161 on October 6, 2011, but the Senate never voted on it, and the EPA cement rules it targeted stayed in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill wipes out a 2010 EPA rule limiting mercury, acid gases, and other toxic air pollution from Portland cement kilns, along with related rules for kilns that burn commercial and industrial waste. It treats those rules as if they never took effect, orders the EPA to write replacement rules within 15 months, and forbids compliance deadlines earlier than five years after the replacement rules take effect. It also directs the EPA to impose the least burdensome option and to adopt narrower definitions of what counts as regulated solid waste.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of Portland cement plants and kilns that burn industrial waste gain the most: they avoid paying for pollution controls on the schedule the 2010 rule required, since compliance cannot begin until at least five years after replacement rules are finalized. Equipment costs, monitoring, and potential plant shutdowns of older kilns are pushed years into the future.

how_it_helps.text: Declares the 2010 EPA emission standards for Portland cement plants and related 2011 waste-burning rules to have no force or effect, as though they had never taken effect.

Requires replacement regulations to be finalized 15 months after enactment, with compliance dates no earlier than five years after the replacement rules' effective date — pushing the earliest compliance roughly six to seven years out.

Directs the EPA to impose the least burdensome regulatory alternative and to ensure standards can be met under actual operating conditions, and to weigh costs, equipment availability, and employment when setting compliance dates.
Requires the EPA to adopt narrower definitions of commercial and industrial waste from a 2000 rule, limiting which burned materials count as regulated solid waste.

analysis.who_pays: People who live, go to school, or work near cement kilns bear the cost: cement kilns are a top source of airborne mercury, which accumulates in soil and water and harms brain development in fetuses and young children, and the bill delays the emission cuts and any nearby-source protections for years. Communities would also wait longer for notice when nearby facilities' pollution regulation is delayed.

drawbacks.text: The bill voids final rules retroactively and restarts the regulatory clock, so toxic emission reductions that had already been ordered are delayed by years, with the burden falling on the communities near the roughly 100 cement kilns nationwide.

A Democratic motion to recommit that would have sped up protections for infants, children, and pregnant women near cement kilns within five miles of schools, day care centers, playgrounds, or hospitals failed 176-247.

Supporters' case is cost and feasibility: the bill requires compliance dates that account for control equipment availability, permit timelines, and jobs, and mandates standards achievable under real operating conditions rather than laboratory conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings go to a single, concentrated industry in the form of deferred capital spending, while the costs are health risks spread across the communities that live around cement kilns — including the fetal and childhood developmental risks from mercury. The bill's defenders argue the 2010 rule's deadlines were not achievable in practice and that a slower schedule protects industrial jobs; its critics note the bill does not merely adjust deadlines but voids finished rules outright and resets them. On the record, the bill trades a several-year delay in toxic emission cuts for industry cost relief.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 262-161 in October 2011, but the Senate never voted on it; it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended, so the EPA rules it would have voided were never wiped out by this bill.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 28, 2011 by Rep. John Sullivan and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The committee approved it 33-12 in a September 21, 2011 markup and reported it amended on September 26.

Democrats offered more than a dozen amendments on the floor — including ones from Waxman, Rush, Schakowsky, Pallone, and others — and each was rejected, most on voice votes sustained against recorded-vote demands.

The House rejected a motion to recommit with instructions to protect infants, children, and pregnant women from toxic air pollutants near cement kilns within five miles of schools, day care centers, playgrounds, and hospitals with maternity or neonatal units, 176-247.
The bill passed the House 262-161, with 237 of 241 Republicans voting yes and 159 of 192 Democrats voting no.
The Senate received the bill on October 11, 2011, read it twice, and placed it on the legislative calendar, where it stayed; no vote ever occurred before the 112th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cement plant owners gained a multi-year window in the House — but because the bill died on the Senate calendar, the people better off in the end were the communities near cement kilns, who kept the emission standards the bill would have voided.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split almost entirely by party — 237 of 241 Republicans voted yes versus 25 of 192 Democrats; the failed motion to recommit drew 175 of 192 Democrats for and 238 of 241 Republicans against.

industries.note: The bill voids the 2010 EPA standards for mercury, acid gases, and other toxic pollutants from cement kilns and pushes compliance at least five years past replacement rules, saving plant owners years of pollution-control spending while communities near kilns keep breathing the emissions in the meantime.

industries.industry: Cement kilns burning commercial and industrial waste
industries.note: The bill wipes out the 2011 waste-burning rules as applied to cement plants and requires adoption of looser 2000-era definitions of what counts as regulated solid waste, letting more burned waste streams escape incinerator-grade emission controls.

By delaying the compliance deadline, the bill postpones demand for the scrubbers, filters, and mercury controls cement plants would otherwise have to buy — a smaller loss, but one that runs alongside the public's interest in faster cleanup.
